Rules / Cleanup

SK0231 The string call produces the string it was given

ToString() on a string, foreach over ToCharArray(), string.Format of a literal with no placeholders, an interpolated string with no holes, and a verbatim prefix that escapes nothing.

CategoryCleanup
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0
ReSharperRedundantToStringCall (resharper_redundant_to_string_call_highlighting)

Why

Two of the five are allocations rather than noise. s.ToCharArray() copies the whole string so that foreach can walk what string already enumerates by index, and string.Format runs a format parser over a format that has no items. The other three are the reader's cost: a $ promises a hole, a @ promises something that needs escaping, and a .ToString() on a string promises a conversion. Each one is a sentence that turns out to say nothing, and a reader has to finish it before finding that out.

Example

Instead of:

foreach (var c in line.ToCharArray()) {
    Consume(c);
}

var label = string.Format("unnamed") + name.ToString();

Write:

foreach (var c in line) {
    Consume(c);
}

var label = "unnamed" + name;

When it does not fire

⚠ Each branch is guarded by what the deletion would mean, not by what it would look like. An interpolated string is reported only where the compiler was converting it to string: FormattableString fs = $"a"; and every interpolated-string-handler overload accept $"a" and reject "a", and nothing in the syntax separates the two. string.Format is reported only where the literal holds no brace at all, because string.Format("{{0}}") returns {0} and the literal returns {{0}} — the shape that looks most obviously safe is the one that is not. A verbatim prefix is reported only where the body holds no backslash, no doubled quote and no newline, since the prefix is what makes each of those mean what it means. ⚠ s.ToString(); as a whole statement is the null-check idiom and is never reported: the result is discarded, so the dereference is the call, and s; is not an expression statement. ⚠ A receiver the compiler's flow analysis says may be null is left alone in both call shapes, because s.ToString() is typed string where s is string? and the deletion is where CS8600 would come from. ⚠ Three of the family's eight inspections are deliberately not covered. RedundantToStringCallForValueType is not: $"{d}" on an IFormattable calls ToString(null, provider) where d.ToString() calls ToString(), and a supplied provider makes those two different strings. RedundantStringInterpolation's single-hole form is not: $"{x}" is "" where x is null and x is null, which is a change of value and not of spelling. RedundantVerbatimPrefix's identifier form is not covered either — it neighbours SK2034. ⚠ `RedundantStringType` is not a C# inspection at all, and reading only the export is what made it look like one: JetBrains' own page for it is about a resource entry in a `.resx` file, where naming the string type restates the default entry type. There is no C# code shape behind it, so it is refuted rather than outstanding. ⚠ The receiver's type is read from the symbol and never from the written name, so ((object)s).ToString() and count.ToString() are both left alone.
